title: The astrolabe
hook: an instrument to find time, direction and the qiblah by the stars

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn al-Haytham: a dark room, a few lamps, and light coming into the eye. Your line was: test it.

It's night in a desert town. No clock on the wall, no phone in a pocket. A man steps into the courtyard holding a disk of brass, hung from a ring on his thumb. He lifts it to his eye, sights a bright star along a little bar on the back, and reads a mark on the rim. Then he turns the disk over and rotates a lacy brass cutout on the front until that star's pointer sits at the height he just read. Now he can read the hour. He can tell which way is north, and which way faces Makkah. A whole sky, folded into his hand. It's called the astrolabe.
screen: `A BRASS DISK ON A THUMB RING.` → `SIGHT A STAR.` → `READ THE HOUR.`

segments.voice: The astrolabe is older than Islam; Greek writers described it. But in the Muslim world it was refined, written about and made beautiful. On the back is a sighting bar, to measure how high the sun or a star stands above the horizon. On the front is a plate engraved with lines for the latitude where you live, and over it turns an open brass web, often called in Arabic al-ankabut, the spider, with little pointers for bright stars. Set the spider so your star sits at the height you just measured, and the instrument shows you the time, and where the sky will be. The Qur'an says that God has set the stars for people so they may guide their way by them in the darkness of land and sea. For people who pray at set times and face the Kaaba in Makkah, that guidance mattered every day. Some mosques kept a timekeeper, called the muwaqqit, whose work was to find the times of prayer from the sun and the stars. And makers took pride in the craft. Ibn al-Nadim, writing a catalog of books and scholars in Baghdad, names an astrolabe maker of Aleppo, a woman called al-Ijliya, who worked for its ruler. The brass is engraved with star names, some of them Arabic, and some of those names still sit on our star maps. The stars tell the time, if you know how to read them.
screen: `OLDER THAN ISLAM, REFINED IN IT.` · `THE SIGHTING BAR AND THE SPIDER.` · `STARS SET FOR GUIDANCE.` · `THE TIMEKEEPER AND THE MAKERS.` · then, large: `THE STARS TELL THE TIME.`

segments.voice: If you know which way north is from where you're sitting, turn your face toward it; if you don't, make a guess. Feel the directions around you, north, east, south, west, as if you stood in that courtyard with the brass disk. If you pray, you can bring to mind the direction you face in prayer; if not, just let the sky be big.
The astrolabe. A brass disk that measures the height of a star and turns it into the hour, the direction, and the qiblah. Today's word.
Your line: the stars tell the time. A whole sky, folded into a hand. Day nine hundred twenty-six, done.
